source.title: An Adaptive Learning Rate Deep Learning Optimizer Using Long and Short-Term Gradients Based on G–L Fractional-Order Derivative
source.authors: Shuang Chen; Changlun Zhang; Hai-Bing Mu

record.tranche_reason: The study compares optimizers on held-out task metrics, a conceptual test of V4; it does not measure the training–test gap directly.
record.gate_note: The optimizer comparison tables report held-out metrics. Introductory discussion of adaptive optimizers and cited prior studies is not counted as a result.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own Adam-versus-SGD held-out comparisons on CIFAR-10 and Penn TreeBank, directly bearing on V4. Training–test gaps are unnecessary for this comparison. Its fixed/default hyperparameters do not reproduce the original tuning protocol.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase accurately describes the authors' performance conclusions: AdaGL converges quickly, exceeds plain SGD on both CIFAR-10 architectures, and achieves the lowest reported test perplexity at every LSTM depth. Add that FracM and FCSGD_G–L outperform AdaGL on CIFAR-10. The authors' assertion that other adaptive methods never exceed SGD conflicts with DenseNet121 diffGrad results.
record.recipe_differences: Compares a newly proposed optimizer with existing optimizers using task-level held-out metrics; does not reproduce the original studies' optimizer-tuning protocols.
record.method_sensitivity: Optimizer ranking varies by task and architecture: CIFAR10 ResNet34 versus DenseNet121 and Penn TreeBank LSTM depth.
record.code_released: Code could be make available at a later stage.
record.problems: The paper reports held-out performance, not train–test gaps; optimizer learning rates and source-code default optimal settings differ across methods, limiting direct attribution to optimizer choice. No significance tests are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant optimizer test-score rows were left out from Tables 2 and 7. Other task results in Tables 4–6 concern graph classification or image generation and do not test the image-classification/language-model settings named in V4.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label versus random-label held-out performance.
Width sweeps beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and learned local connectivity.
Controlled comparisons of limited versus broader tuning, decoupled weight decay, switching to SGD, and quantified equality or superiority of training performance alongside held-out differences.
Batch-size sweeps under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove batch penalties.
Dropout interventions and their interactions with dataset size, augmentation and weight decay.
Measured magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps and comparisons with other generalization measures.
Removing memorized examples versus random examples and retraining.

missing.what: Eighteen omitted adaptive-optimizer comparisons. At one/two/three layers, SGD perplexities are 85.07/67.42/63.55; Yogi 86.59/71.33/67.51; AdaBound 84.78/67.53/63.58; diffGrad 81.18/64.68/59.98; AdaBelief 84.21/66.29/61.23; AdaDerivative 90.40/75.25/71.70; FCAdam_G–L 85.16/64.71/60.26. The record incorrectly states that no relevant Table 7 rows were omitted.

record.verdict_notes: All extracted numerical values match the supplied tables. CIFAR-10 uses fixed initial learning rates, a shared decay schedule and source-code defaults; language-model adaptive learning rates are selected between 0.001 and 0.01. These recipes limit attribution to optimizer choice and do not establish the effects of broader tuning. Reversed row states describe direction relative to the usual adaptive disadvantage; they do not automatically challenge V4, which explicitly permits language-model advantages and conditional exceptions.

versions.untested_parts: Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
Broad tuning, decoupled weight decay, switching from Adam to SGD, and the full range of image-classification and language benchmarks.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout comparisons and interactions with data augmentation or weight decay.
Sharpness and other measured properties of trained networks.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.

tranche.reason: The study directly compares held-out optimizer performance using its own recipes rather than reproducing the original optimizer-tuning protocol.

source_check.notes: Table 2 uncertainties are standard deviations; Table 7 provides no uncertainty. The authors' assertion that other adaptive methods do not surpass SGD conflicts with DenseNet121 diffGrad; reversed Adam row states describe the main disadvantage direction while supporting V4's explicit language-model exception.

statements.correction: Table 7 test PPL, Adam/SGD: 1 layer=84.28/85.07; 2 layers=67.27/67.42; 3 layers=64.28/63.55. Adam advantage=depth-dependent; V4 language-model exception=supported at 1 and 2 layers; universal language-model advantage=not claimed.
statements.problem: The depth-dependent Adam ordering and numbers are correct, but a challenges label overstates the implication: V4 explicitly allows Adam to do better on word-level language models without promising an advantage at every depth.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Adam on ResNet34 and Adam on 3-layer LSTM; FCAdam_G–L on DenseNet121
reader_labels.reason: These adaptive methods have worse test metrics than SGD in these settings (R2, R9, R18).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Adaptive optimizer comparisons across CIFAR10 classifiers and Penn TreeBank LSTMs
reader_labels.reason: Results are mixed: diffGrad beats SGD on DenseNet121, Adam beats SGD on the 1-layer LSTM, and AdaGL beats SGD on both image models and all three LSTM sizes (R3, R5, R8, R10, R12, R13, R15, R16, R19).
